footerNote: Oracle reports its delivery costs as 'Cloud services and license support', 'Hardware' and 'Services' expense lines; those three are combined here as cost of revenue. Segment names follow Oracle's fiscal 2025 presentation; from fiscal 2026 Oracle regrouped its reporting into Cloud, Software, Hardware and Services.

segments.name: Cloud services & license support
segments.note: Renting Oracle's cloud, plus support for the software customers already run — the steady base of the business, 78% of all revenue.

segments.name: Cloud license & on-premise license
segments.note: New software licenses sold outright, for customers running Oracle on their own machines — shrinking as customers move to cloud subscriptions instead.

segments.name: Services
segments.note: Consulting and support services that help customers run Oracle products.

takeaways.text: Remaining performance obligation — contracts signed but not yet delivered — jumped 63% in a year to more than $130B. Oracle said the first Stargate contract, the giant AI-infrastructure project, had not even been signed yet.
takeaways.title: The backlog jumped 63%

takeaways.text: Cloud infrastructure revenue (IaaS — renting computing power) grew 49% to $2.7B, and total cloud revenue rose 23% to $6.2B. AI training workloads are the driver: customers rent Oracle's data centers to build and run AI models.
takeaways.title: Cloud infrastructure is the growth engine

takeaways.text: New on-premise license sales fell 10% to $1.13B. That is the old Oracle shrinking on schedule — customers who once bought software outright now rent it as a cloud subscription, which shows up in the support line above instead.
takeaways.title: Old license sales keep shrinking

verdict: Oracle's revenue grew 6% to $14.1B and net income rose 22% to $2.94B as cloud kept taking over the mix — and its backlog of signed contracts jumped 63% to more than $130B.
